commits.subject: Lay the foundation: a DOM-free core with tests, and a planet
Make it a site: prerendered pages, the spinning mark, one colour to choose
Start the planet where the pipeline says it starts: an icosahedron
Use the 1999 algorithm, from the source, instead of an approximation of it
Grow the core: a shell over the site, two simulations, and the markdown the pages need
Wire the browser: a real prompt, the theme, in-page navigation, three programs, the favicon
Lay the foundations, on three lines
Let the still favicon be a planet too
Let a page insist on its sky: the worlds are always night, with stars
Turn the sky: slowly on its own, and with the hand that turns the world
On a page that keeps its own theme, hide the button and let the command say so
Slide the sky, do not spin it: a turn of the world moves the stars sideways, a tilt up or down
A sky that neither repeats nor slides away: big seeded tiles, and the background moves, not the layer
Give the world inertia, send the sky with the hand, and let theme auto mean system
The surface follows the hand: the renderer turns the other way, so the drag is subtracted
The climate and the paint of 1999, from the source: summits are cold wherever they stand
The colours come back; the climate keeps the 1999 shape, so a summit is white wherever it stands
A phone is 20rem wide: the navigation takes a second line, and nothing is wider than the screen
The stars move by transform, so the browser stops redrawing the sky
The rasteriser keeps its buffers instead of asking for them every frame
The tab's icon is encoded off the drawing thread, and nothing paints unseen
The folders say what the site is, not what kind of file each one holds
A feature brings its own command, and the shell stops knowing what a theme is
The sky is its own feature, and follows the world without either knowing it
Draw the architecture, and make a test the reason it stays drawn correctly
The prompt learns the three keys a person's hands already know
theme says where it landed, and offers the two it did not take
Two things adding a page turned up: a stale shell, and a word too long
Two passes over a line, so a link may hold code and emphasis may hold a link
theme offers the commands themselves, not two bare words
The em dash survives the line it was wrapped onto
Measured the tab icon, and took the change back out
Code is coloured at build time, by a tokeniser written here
Diagrams are drawn at build time, by a layout engine written here
The page is a session: ls in the header, the command that printed each page, and a prompt with its cursor as the last line
The cursor stands where the caret is, the suggestion after it, and a new page starts with a clean screen
The frame is set in the machine's type, the words in the author's, and the column is seventy-two of its columns
The session opens on one line: @drpicox ~ $ ls
The prompt keeps to the bottom of the window, and the page fills it
The name is a little larger than its line, and the line does not grow for it
The paper is the console: what the shell says is printed on the page, under a rule the prompt keeps
The paper ends on its prompt, the footer comes after the session, and cat prints a page like any other
The prompt line runs from edge to edge, on a ground a shade off the paper
The session moves and the paper stays: cd and cat carry the address, the typed line shows on the paper, and the titles are in the machine's type
The ghost stays on its line, the machine's type is set tighter, and the first key brings the paper to the line
A trial: the world in the header drawn in character cells, in the sixteen colours of a text-mode card
The home headline is typed over: a cursor, then the words taken back a character at a time and another line typed
clear clears the paper; the headlines come in rounds, three lines each, and lead somewhere
A linked headline says so with an arrow, not a line under it
Open data kept a year at a time: NO2 from the air-quality network, asked for only when the year has changed
NO2 by the hour and the month: the table is in the HTML, the choices arrive with the script
Weather kept a year at a time: histograms of the daily extremes and the rain at nine stations, checked against the pipeline they came from
One bar a year, drawn once: the NO2 years and the weather's share a chart in the frame
The axis of years drawn once, under bars that start at zero and dots that need not
Hot nights, counted: days over a threshold at nine stations, the still in the HTML, the source line under every figure
The programs tested as a reader uses them; the deploy keeps the year it fetched; the decisions written down
NO2 wears its good-to-bad colours again, and the Observatori Fabra stands green above the city
Poblenou is what a reader sees first, and the Palau Reial joins the stations
The next word: a language model reduced to counting and dice, its first moment in the HTML; programs are handed the site they stand in
A relativistic rocket: the sums of the Rocinante Simulator, checked against the Physics FAQ's table, with the original a link away
What strangers install: npm's counts kept a year at a time, a line for each package that earned one
code/ becomes open-source/, with the npm packages in it; sections open with what is in them; a page that moves says where it was
The thesis's measurements, drawn: an hour and a quarter became under two minutes on eighteen watts
The toggle keeps its place on a page that keeps its own theme; theme answers with all three choices, each with its sign
The rocket gets its sky: the stars within twelve light-years, turning, and the ship flying the chosen trip with its two clocks
Teaching opens with both courses; a bars block draws a few numbers at build time; emphasis may hold a code span; the first half of the thesis, in numbers
The larger machine of the thesis, measured: the GT 430 beside the i7, each machine held against its own single thread
Loops into zones: the method of the thesis, step by step; the years chosen on the NO2 page stay when the station changes
Diagrams may go round: state machines for the lock and for a line of the buffer pool; the bar that went the wrong way, and the lock the next bar reveals
The shell says what things are and can look for them: ls with titles, help that folds, find and grep; C and Java coloured; diagram rows keep their balance
ls offers .. everywhere but the root, and pressing it is a cd
The worlds are from around 2000: the oldest copy that survives is January 2001, and 1999 was memory
Sixty-four rooms: the text adventure of a first-year lab, rule for rule, playable, with its map
The program that finished before the professor left: the bird-card parser of 1999, and what its rules show; Prolog coloured
The post compiler, live: a post on the left, the test and the context it writes on the right, and the compiler's refusals in its own words
The interaction test breaks the rule the compiler checks second, not the one it checks first
The adventure speaks English, word for word from the Spanish, which stays beside it as the source
find walks the tree in order and lines its titles up; ls sorts by name with -n and turns round with -r
The worlds are from 2000: the record places the course in the autumn term of 2000
The fish auction of December 2000: the Dutch auction, Vicente on the clearing margin, Wanda and the planner read back, and a seat for the visitor's own agent
The fishing lagoon of the 2018 lab: a commons that breeds, the starter's bots and its tit for tat, and a seat for the visitor's own
Formulas as MathML from a small notation in a math fence, and the board says, box by box, the price every buyer was ready to shout at
The maze of the VRML course, May 2001: its dig grown again from Java's own random, wall for wall against the file it wrote, and the spheres that led nowhere
The first network joins main: letters told apart by backpropagation, and the robot of 1995 that looks for the light

Seven directories in two bands instead of twelve in the order they were made; simulators, worlds and open data under projects and the kata under teaching, each leaving its old address; links, so a lab can stand in projects too; and a home that says what the site is and lists what each directory holds
The first network joins main again without the QBasic: the class it was shown to, the PC carried from home, and letters of the visitor's own for it to learn
A listing is one column of names, as wide as the longest, so every title starts where the one above it does
The Fibergochi of February 1999, playable again: a student of the FIB kept like a Tamagotchi, with its own drawings, its rules as they were, and its words in English
The Fibergochi lives a step every half second, a term in ten minutes, slow enough to look after; and its drawings are mine, pixel by pixel
The Fibergochi's three lamps say what they are: exam, lab and terminal, written under the drawing instead of hidden in a tooltip
The Fibergochi's lamps go back beside the drawing, say what they are on hover or on a press, and the date has under it how much there is to study, how much lab work, and whether it holds a terminal
The Fibergochi asks for all 39 drawings at once, where nobody sees them, and turns frames in the same picture, so it no longer blinks while a drawing loads
The Fibergochi is the version of 2 March 1999 that was online: the bar, friends, stress, begging that works, the alfa score, a class in the VAX room, habits, three speeds and its own key drawings

A rocket short of fuel shares it between its two burns by mass ratio, not by weight: it now stops with an empty tank, goes faster with more fuel and a faster exhaust, and no longer jumps where it stops having to coast
The rocket page shows the Rocinante Simulator it comes from, and the two books behind it: The Expanse, whose ship gives it its name, and Project Hail Mary, whose Tau Ceti is now a trip to fly

A demonstration can be a Program, an input and an output: the build runs it for its still, the shell as a command, the page again whenever a dial moves. Technical debt is the first, and its page now has its figure in the HTML
The rocket is a program too, with its destination a choice: rocket --to tau-ceti at the prompt, and on its page the star map stands around the program's own dials, hearing what it ran with

An agent in the reader's browser is offered the site through WebMCP: every program as a tool whose schema is its parameters, which moves the dials the reader is looking at and answers with the figures, and the prompt itself as one more
A tool answers an agent with a string, as Chrome's WebMCP expects, and a refusal is thrown so the agent is told it failed
A refusal is answered in words and not thrown: Chrome replaces a thrown message with its own, and the agent lost the reason it needed to ask again

The home opens on the book, and the book on one dial: a page can show a program small, ::technical-debt --shortcuts, with only the dials it names and the one chart that says the argument. The essays follow

A trial of the home as a portfolio: the essays with their Medium covers and what there is to run with a picture of it running, as cards the width of a program. Off unless asked for, by portfolio at the prompt or ?portfolio=on; the pictures are in the HTML either way and fetched only when shown

Flags are the frame's: a feature declares a trial, and flags lists them all with a switch each, a link turns one on with ?name=on, the choice is kept and marked on the root before paint. The portfolio is the first, and is now only a flag and its stylesheet

Six things to run, so the cards fill two rows, the first network among them; every entry on the home is a title with its line under it, the way the essays page writes them, so a card has no dash left over and an essay card says what the essay argues
A card has no border of its own; its picture has one, with its corners rounded, so a white screenshot on a white page and a dark one on a dark page still have an edge
Merge pull request #18 from drpicox/claude/clever-bardeen-2hejwm

The architecture is read by the compiler: a graph of the source, with whether each arrow needs a value or only a type, now the one architecture.test reads, and two new rules on it — no boxes in a circle, one value exported a file. The circle between plugin and program is broken, and eighteen files that exported more than one value are one each

Pure logic out of browser folders, where it can be tested in node: the keys typed before the prompt could listen, and the scale the feature-size dial slides along. The line carried over a navigation is its own store, the heat grid its own file, and the work week knows the names of its days and hours

How this site is built: its source as boxes and arrows at every commit that changed it, read by the compiler and played on its page — each file a ball that flies where the next commit puts it, the tangle it would be with no boxes, untangled from the top down, and the tests with the files none of them reaches drawn as rings. The last commit is the still, in the HTML

My first neural network, which is what it was; the rocket's card is the Rocinante Simulator in three dimensions; and how this site is built earns a card on the home, in the place of the sixty-four rooms

Point at a file and its own arrows come out, what it needs and what needs it, while everything it is not tied to steps back; a file of nothing but types is not counted against the tests, and the caption says how many of the files with something to test a test reaches

Line coverage, counted by vitest's own reader of V8's count — the fourth devDependency, and why, in DECISIONS.md — and drawn on the architecture page: with the tests in, at the commit it was counted on, each file is a pie as full as the tests run it

The sixty-four rooms drawn as rooms: walls where there is no way out, a door that wants a key marked until it is opened, what each room holds now as a picture, the player standing in it, and the life left as hearts. The game's own words and its status line are as it printed them

flags is laid out as help is, a list that folds on a narrow screen: the switch in the terminal's letters, the one in force standing out, and what it does in words that wrap instead of running off the edge

With the tests in, a test is a green square and a file a blue ball as full as the tests run it, with a legend under the picture to say so; a pale ball for a test was taken for a file, and a red ring for a test

Trials: a flag can be on for a share of readers, drawn once each and kept until they choose, and the portfolio is one in two. GoatCounter counts, once a visit, the side a reader is on and what they open from the home, the theme they arrive with and the one they set, and the commands they run by name alone — never what they typed after it

work/: when a rule matters, I turn it into code instead of a guide, so it holds for a person and for an agent alike — three cases told by their mechanism and not their client (a mask that cannot drift from its audit, a test suite as a language, an agent reliable by construction), changes without surprises, and speed measured before it was touched. One line of it on the home, and one of the headlines
Revert the work/ pages, the line on the home and the headline that led to them: the site is not a CV

craft/: a rule that matters goes into the code, not into a guide — shown in small examples that run here. The first is new: a sentence is a step and the post is the test, read the way my course's platform read it, with what a post becomes in Java and JavaScript, and where the idea went: Gherkin Genie. How this site is built, the course and Raft are linked in beside it

craft/: how I work, as a manifesto — in the code, with others and behind it, each line where it runs or where I argued it; Robert C. Martin's Bowling Game Kata replayed commit by commit, every one run in the page by a Jest-like runner of our own; and the tests of my 2018 essay run against a dispatcher, the same one refactored, and one with a bug where its two halves meet. craft/writing becomes a redirect; the kata's errata, the three testing talks and Raft's hints are said as the sources say them

craft/: every line of the manifesto with the essays where I argued it, [1, 2], and under it what it looks like — a snippet or a quote of my own, word for word; two new lines, small safe steps and the tools I build; small steps as a row that fills at random, a red put right at once, played by a player that pauses, rests and never moves for a reader who asked for less motion; Gherkin Genie in the page, the steps it wishes for and the scenario run once they exist; "the post is the test" becomes "a sentence is a step", tied to the course where the post came first
craft/: the quotes under the points big again, as the site's quotes are; the room between points stays
craft/: small steps — a red is not left red: green rises from below while it waits, and once put right it glows a moment, to be remembered; and the first two pieces of slides, read and typed

Slides: a ```slides block is code in frames, each one what the code became next, with what the tests said — every frame in the HTML, the last one shown; in the browser each is typed from the one before, a caret where the next letter goes, then run, red or green, played once, only on screen, with the same player to pause it or play it again; a storyboard for a reader who asked for less motion. The manifesto's snippets that are stories now play: the perfect game made to fail once, the five steps of add, the rename, the rows of the puzzle, the default an AI added
craft/kata: an invitation in — the way on marked until it is taken, a word that every commit can be clicked, and the way that is not there looking it

craft/kata: beside each step, what my essays on the kata say about it and a link to where they say it at length — step tests that come and go, the simplest rule first, refactor only after it works, add before removing, one aspect at a time, the IDE, not from scratch, the five steps one by one, a test seen failing once; and the five steps as a section of their own, played from the replay's own commits, green after every one. Slides type a new line from the end of the one above, as a person does
craft/kata: the game's state in private fields, #score and #rolls, rather than behind an underscore; and what each commit took away is still there, where it was, struck through

craft/: how a sentence becomes Gherkin Genie's name for it, played step by step — the line copied, the parentheses, the keyword lowered, each word capitalised, the number taken out into its parameter and an N left behind, and the words joined

craft/a-sentence-is-a-step: Gherkin Genie's files and its answer coloured — Gherkin in the highlighter, the steps as JavaScript, and each file to edit laid over its coloured copy, kept in step as it is typed

shell: find with a word finds the pages that say it too, after those with it in the name or title, marked as such; and ls -t prints a directory as the table at the end of its page — the same table, drawn by the same code

sliders: still native, now with room for a finger — as tall as a finger needs, a thumb that can be found, larger on a touch screen, and sideways gestures kept for the slider while the page keeps the vertical ones

projects/architecture: a ball as big as the files that need it, so the hotspots stand out (or as what it needs, or its lines); a reach for a file's arrows — one, two, three or all — its blast radius both ways, with the count at each; what needs a file in orange, never again taken for the blue of what it needs; a file, a box or a commit opens on GitHub as it stood then; and the lines below read in their own units, so a click lands where it is, and they can be dragged along

craft/guess-the-rule: the rule-guessing game my old site had in 2020 for the essay on testing and refactoring, played again — its rules and its words as they were, the old address sending readers here; and the manifesto's 'Assume I got it wrong' pointing to it

home: in the dark theme the cards' pictures are dark too — the tool takes them with THEME=dark, a card titled "card dark" carries both, and the stylesheet shows the one the theme wants, the other never fetched; the light ones taken again, with the sliders as they are now

projects/architecture: the tangle comes to rest — it cools as Fruchterman and Reingold's does, from hot to still, warming a little when a commit brings new files; no file moves further than a step allows, two files on each other push no harder than a limit, and the walls take the speed out of what hits them. With this site's files it had begun to shake for ever
projects/architecture: the crowded tangle's test as crowded as before in half the picture, so it runs in the deploy's time too — with coverage counted there, it had run out of it

projects/architecture: the history knows what each commit changed — every file git saw it edit or move, a file it brought not among them — and it is the main line's, a branch's commits arriving with the merge that brought them. Taken by date, a branch and the main line took turns, and each looked as if it had deleted the other's files

projects/changes: how this site changes — the history read for what changed, how often and with what. Every box at every commit; a file hottest in the commits right after it is written, and most never touched again; the files that never settle, each with its life and how much of it the tests run; Robert C. Martin's instability beside how often a box really changed, warm where the zone of pain hurts; how far a change travels up the arrows against how far they would let it, and whether an arrow onto a type carries less; what changes together with no arrow to say so; and how many changes came with their test. Every figure is in the HTML, and every number in it is read off the history at every push

projects/architecture: a ball can be as big as the commits that have changed it so far, growing as the history plays and stopping where a file settles; every file a commit changes rings as it comes, warm, apart from the blue a new file is born with; and the picture sends to how this site changes

projects/changes: how far a change travels, and what an arrow carries, are read off the arrows each commit found, not the ones it left — what the design offered a change as it was made, which is the fair test of it; an arrow the commit draws has carried nothing yet. The figures hardly move for it. And three sentences say only what the history does: a file is likeliest to change right after it is written, not most of its changes; most of what changes it later comes with new files or a sweep; and a stable box is hard to change, not unable to

projects/changes: the page draws its own figures, so a reader who arrives by a link, without a reload, sees them — the HTML the build wrote held them, a page moved to in the browser held only their places — and it plays its history as the picture of how the site is built does: a player above the figures, staying in sight, takes every one of them to any commit, and they show the source as it stood then; the picture of changes is its line of time too, a commit pressed on it is where they go, and pointing at a cell says which box, which day, and the files that commit changed or wrote there. One table of figures draws the HTML and the page alike

projects/changes: what an independent reading found, put right. An arrow onto a type counts changes to the type itself, not to what is behind it — that is what the figure of how far a change travels shows — and when one file is most of such arrows the caption says so, with what it and the rest carried; the history cannot say which way a change went, only that files joined by arrows change together; a box's changes leave the sweeps out; a hotspot is often changed and large, as Adam Tornhill has it; the list of hot files is dated; and a file that comes to hold nothing but types, or stops, is known so, as the history now records

projects/architecture: the source read as a graph, and as a history on it, in node and tested — the groups the arrows make by the Louvain method and their modularity against the boxes'; how much each file stands between the others, by Brandes' algorithm; how far a change to each could reach; which box arrows go against the rule of stable dependencies, and each box's two couplings, Ca and Ce, file by file; how hot each file is at a commit; where each file stood at each commit, and from it the cascade and what each file's ground made likely; the threads of what changed together, with what joins them; and the lenses the picture will be seen through, worked out whole for any commit

projects/architecture, projects/changes: the picture of the source seen through lenses, on both pages — a ball as big as what needs it, what it needs, how far a change to it could reach, how much it stands between the others, the commits that changed it or its lines; coloured by how lately it changed, by what the changes below it made likely, or by how stable its box is, with the arrows against the rule of stable dependencies in red; threads between the files that changed together, dashed where no arrow joins them, pulling them together in the tangle; and pointing at a file brings out its arrows, its group or what changed with it. On the page of how the site changes the picture follows the page's player, seen through the changes; on the page of how it is built it leads the figures of what the tangle shows — its groups against the boxes, its bridges, how far a change could reach, commit by commit. And the page of changes gains what the ground of each file made likely against what it did, and Ca and Ce drawn for any box, with the sum worked out

projects/architecture, projects/changes: what a second independent reading found, put right. What a file's ground would lead one to expect now counts every commit at its own share, nothing changed below among them, so a file that changed as the history's rates say stands on the line, and three arrows away and further are one distance, since few changes are seen there; it says where a file stood, not what moved it, and the pages no longer say a file inherits anything. A bridge stands on a share of the shortest ways read either way, which says where the source meets, not what a change would cross; the Louvain method is said as what it does; the groups count the features that are a group to themselves, whole; heat and changes leave the sweeps out; exposure is scaled over the files there are; Martin counts classes, a file standing for one; the dated sentence is dated. And the picture on the page of changes works out a commit only when it is on screen, and the cascade's type stands in a file of its own, with no circle left between two files

projects/architecture: the source read as a network, in node and tested — how deep in the knot each file sits, its core (Seidman, 1983); how tall the stack of what it needs; how far apart the files are and how near each is to the rest, walked from every file on arrays; how clustered, file by file and as a whole (Watts and Strogatz, 1998); whether files with many links join files with few (Newman, 2002); each file's place by PageRank; the parts and the circles, by Tarjan's algorithm, which the rule on boxes now reads too; the network as a whole against a random one as big, and its small-world-ness (Humphries and Gurney, 2008); and, for any file at any commit, where it stands in all of them and what its history has been. The life of a file on a line stands in a file of its own, for the hotspots and what comes next

projects/architecture, projects/changes: the details of a file or a box by the picture, and the network it makes. No word is drawn over the picture any more: what pointing at a file brings out is said on a line above it, keyed by colour, where it covers no arrow. A click chooses a file or a box, ringed and kept brought out until it is let go, and the panel by the picture tells of it at the commit shown — where a file stands in the network: what it needs and what a change to it could reach, how much it stands between the others, its place by PageRank, shared where files rank alike, how far it is from the rest, how deep in the knot, its group and its box; its history, from the commit that wrote it to the files it changed with and what its ground would lead one to expect; a box's couplings with the sum worked out — every file and box it names a way to its own details, and a link to the code as it stood then; with nothing chosen, the network as a whole, and the files it hinges on. On a phone the panel stands under the picture, and a tap brings it into view. The page on how the site is built opens what the tangle shows with the network: how its links are spread, on log scales, and the source against a random network as big, a small world (Watts and Strogatz, 1998; Humphries and Gurney, 2008), what that number says and what it does not. What an independent reading found is put right before it went out: the clustering said as the average it is, the blast radius only one way, and no fit claimed that was not made

The harness: no feature imports another, a ratchet on the shape of the source, and the contracts no import states held by tests. The sky no longer imports the world: it says what it can follow, in its own words, and the composition hands it what the world announces — skyFeature(turning), in the list of features, where the compiler checks that the two agree; delete either and the other still builds. The architecture test now fails when a feature imports another, and when two files, not only two boxes, need each other round in a circle. A ratchet holds where the shape of the source stands — the box arrows against stability, the composition's aside; the deepest core; the tallest stack; the files with something to run that no test imports — and fails when one gets worse, and when one gets better and is not written in. And every two files that changed together three times with nothing joining them need a test that imports both: the page the build writes and the terminal and the navigation that take it over now have one, which fails when the prompt, the title, the main or the lit link would differ from what a load gives, and ls and find have one for the order and the look of their lists. The deploy checks the contracts again once it has written the history. The page on how the site is built, the diagrams and the rules say so

projects/architecture: the ratchet, on the page. What a ratchet is and why it starts where the source is, and the file that holds it, linked; and a figure of the four measures it holds — the box arrows against stability, the composition's aside; the deepest core; the tallest stack; the files with something to run that no test imports — each with what it counts, how it went at every commit of the history, measured as the ratchet measures it now, and where it stands at the commit shown, which at the last one is what the file keeps. A dashed line marks the commit that brought the ratchet in, and the caption says since when it holds them and whether any has gone up since

projects/architecture: the ratchet and the source, side by side, and how the ratchet went. The history now keeps what architecture.ratchet.json held, read at every commit and kept only where it changed, so the page no longer has to know which commit brought it in. For each measure the figure sets what the ratchet holds beside what the source measures, at the commit shown, as two numbers; over the history, what it held is a band that steps wherever the file was changed, and what the source measured is the line inside it, the commits before the ratchet as well. Under them, how the ratchet went: when it began and what it held, and every time since it was tightened, or loosened; and whether at any commit since it began the source measured more than it held. On a phone each measure takes two lines

research: two experiments since the thesis, from Medium. Coverage, generated: a program that knows nothing of what the code is for wrote the tests, a final-degree project Gerard Torrent took on, and reached 85% code coverage, step by step against the 80% many companies ask for; why coverage is for the programmer and says nothing to a manager. The language of the question: the same questions to the same AI in Catalan, Spanish, English, French and Dutch, first ChatGPT 3.5 on a row at the Oscars, then Claude on dubbing and on tourism, with the two tables of what each language answered, and what it means. The markdown the site writes in has tables now: a row between pipes, a head over a line of dashes, and a wrapper so one wider than a phone scrolls by itself

The deploy reports how the shape of the source moved with each push, in the summary of its run: the files and the arrows, what the ratchet holds — each marked better or worse, since lower is better for all of them — and how the network reads, from the commit the push started from to the last. It is there to be read, not to pass; the ratchet is the test. node tools/shape-report.mjs prints the same at a desk

The deploy breaks, on purpose, the lines each push changed: one small change at a time — === into !==, && into ||, >= into <, true into false, a step by one the other way — made in code only, never in a string, a template or a comment, nor in a generic or a shift; the tests that import each file are run, and what no test caught goes into the summary of the run. Code coverage says a line was run; this says whether running it was checked, which is what coverage as a target cannot. Run at a desk, node tools/mutate.mjs breaks what is not committed yet. It found, first thing, what its own tests and the shape report's did not check: an escaped quote in a string, a truth followed by something, a commit the history does not have, and the marks of what the ratchet holds, which now come from one list

The agent's harness, as Claude Code hooks in the repository. After every edit to a file of the source, the agent is told what the history knows of it: how often it changed, what it usually changes with and, where no arrow joins the two, whether a test holds what they agree on, what needs it and how far a change to it could reach, and the tests that import it — the panel beside the picture, said at the moment it matters. And a turn cannot end while what is not committed leaves the type check or the tests red: the agent is told what is red, a state found green is remembered in .git and not checked again, and the same red is held at most twice, since one the agent cannot mend is for the person to see. The page on how the site is built says so, with the mutations the deploy makes, and why coverage alone would not do

The frame, sorted by how often things change: what a command is, what running one asks of the page, and that said as plain text now stand in platform/command, apart from the shell, since the features, the programs and the flags agree on them and the boxes everything needs should need nothing that changes as often as the shell does; the terminal, the shell's face in the browser, stands in platform/shell/browser, and the move between pages, which writes the page's main again, in platform/page/browser, so that platform/browser, which every feature's browser code needs, no longer needs the shell or the page. Box arrows against stability go from eight to five, and the ratchet holds five; the five left are the contract of a feature needing the types of what a feature brings. The diagrams and the rules say where things are

The contracts no import states, held from the second time: two files of different boxes that changed together twice with nothing joining them need a test that imports both. Within a box, changing together is what makes it one, and a pair whose agreement the compiler holds — two implementations of Program, which grow together when it does — is listed in the test with why. Three contracts that were only kept by hand are now written down where breaking them fails: the theme the head's script paints before anything shows and the one the theme's own script settles, for every choice a reader can have made and a page that insists; the list at the end of a directory's page and what ls -t prints there, in the author's order; and the technical-debt simulation as the home shows it, with only the dial the page names and its glance. The ratchet holds one untested file fewer

projects/architecture: the picture's two biggest files, a part each taken out and tested. The panel beside the picture stands on its own: it says what is chosen at the commit shown, draws itself again only when that changed, keeps open the commits the reader opened while the history moves on, waits for a dragged slider to stop, and hands every name in it to whoever chooses; tested in the page. And which arrows pointing at a file brings out — one step further out each time, and only along the way each was found — is worked out in node and tested, and the scene only draws them

Tests for eight files that changed and had none, the most changed first among those a test can hold in node: a bar chart draws a bar for every value, standing on the axis and as long as its value; a line chart runs every series across the whole width, the highest at the top; cd moves the session and the address, goes home and up, and lands through a link where the page really is; cat prints a page by README.md, by * or by its directory's name, and finds no other file; help lines every command up with what it does; the features installed have names of their own, and bring no command, program or place a name another already has — nor one of the site's own; and the page of changes, before any script, stands at the last commit and draws every place it names. The ratchet holds eight untested files fewer. Two of the claims were mine and wrong, and the code was right: help pads to the longest usage, and cat takes a directory's name for its page
changeStills.test: a still is handed the dials its place names as well, none here; the type check, which the last commit did not wait for, is clean again

The deploy was red since the frame was sorted, and it was right: with the history written again, the move between pages and what a command answers stand in boxes of their own now, and the history says they changed together, twice and more, with the shell and its commands, with no test to hold what they agree on. It is held now: the shell decides where cd and cat lead, and the page goes there without a load, keeping what was printed, the same as the shell answers in node; cat prints in the page what it prints there; and a command's name that help prints runs where it is, on the same page. At a desk the history was from before the move, so its new paths were not in it, and the check could not see them; the history in public/data is written again to 293295e

A commit is not let through while the source is red. A Claude Code hook before every shell command that commits runs the type check and the tests, as the hook before the end of a turn does, and says what is red instead of committing: what is committed is what the deploy builds, and a red commit is a failed deploy the next commit has to mend. Both ask the same question of the same place, remembering a state found green; and the checks that read the history read it as the deploy will write it, with the work not committed yet as one more commit — the tool writes that history where asked, never over what is committed, and the architecture test reads the one it is handed. A move between boxes, which the history at a desk could not see until it was committed, is seen before

world: what has no purpose goes. quantizeToVga came with the trial of the world drawn in character cells, which takes each cell to the card's colours with nearestVga, and nothing in the site took a whole picture to them: only its own test ran it, so it goes, and that test with it. positionOf, where a vertex sits in space, is what the pipeline never needs and the claims about the sphere do: it lives in their test now, not as a module of the site. Code no test runs asks whether it is hard to test, has no purpose, or has one no test states; these two answered the second

What no test runs, as a question and not as a number. Coverage now keeps what it counted function by function, and the deploy says, in the summary of its run, which functions and lines no test runs, under the question each file asks: nothing in the site uses it, so it has no purpose, or only a test's — remove it, or move it into the test; only a browser runs it, so it is hard to test where it is — test it in a page, or move what it decides out of the browser; or the site uses it and no test runs it — a behaviour no test states, to write, or code with none worth stating, to remove. The first answer of the third kind is written: of every page, every place it names has a program to run it or a still to stand in it, and every still fills its place as the build fills it, which the build, swallowing a still that fails, had never been made to prove

An agent is answered the same way by every tool, and told whether the reader saw it. A tool is written in node now, as an AgentTool in plugin/: what it takes, and an answer in one shape — summary, data with its units in its names, the page as a url, and, for figures someone else publishes, source and refreshed; the browser only registers it and decides whether to show. A tool that has something to show takes a show, true unless the agent says otherwise: false answers and leaves the reader's page as it is, and the answer's shown says which happened, so an agent never has to guess what the reader has in front of them. Besides the programs, the site offers what is about itself, in agent/: read, a page as the markdown it is written in with the pages under it, and search, the pages that say every word asked with the lines that say them — neither writes a line at the reader's prompt nor moves anything on their screen, where the shell, which stays, fills the paper. The rocket answers with the trip it was asked for and not every trip, and its speeds say they are shares of light. The shell's tool names the commands that get around the site, and a test holds that the shell has them

writings: what David has written and said, as a tool for an agent, read off the pages that list them. The essays page and the talks page are the list — a link and a line under a subject for each essay, a dated line for each talk — so there is no second list to keep: a page changed is the tool changed, and a test reads the real pages to hold that every essay and every dated talk on them is read. An agent asks for essays, talks or both, about some words, and talks of some years; the essays are not dated here, so years are for talks. What the pages do not list, the answer says where to find: the essays on Medium, by the first link of the essays page, and the talks page for the ones without a date. A feature can bring a tool of its own now, beside its programs

llms.txt: the site as an agent with no browser is told of it — whose it is, every page by its address and its summary under the directory it stands in, and the tools a browser with WebMCP is offered, with what each takes and how every one answers. Without it, an agent that cannot call the tools could not tell they were there. It is written at build time, and served the same in dev, from the same pages and the same tools as everything else, so it cannot fall behind them

The comments on the agent's tools, gone over. Showing is the default because work the reader cannot watch is done on a different site from theirs, and the option not to show is there to compare many answers without taking the reader through as many pages — the comment had kept only the first half, which the option contradicted. A read-only tool changes nothing the site holds, and no more is claimed: showing may take the reader to another page, as a link would, and what a page held unsaved goes with it. How every answer is shaped is said once for all tools so none can describe it otherwise; and search's limits say what each is enough for

The year still running, on the hot nights page: in grey, to the last day the Meteocat has, and kept out of every mean and both halves. It was left out on purpose — half a bar at the end of a chart is misinformation made of correct numbers — and David wanted it, so it is shown and shown to be unfinished: grey, not the outline a year with holes gets, its bar saying the day it reaches, the line under the figure saying it too. It is kept in a file of its own, running.json, never committed: it changes every day, and a commit back from every deploy would leave the main line behind wherever it was pushed from. The build asks for it once a day at most, keeps yesterday's when the portal fails, and in January shows last year until the portal has its December; in CI, with no copy, at every deploy, and a weekly run keeps it from getting more than a week old when nobody pushes. A source says how to read a year so far beside how to read a whole one; the weather reads it with the same checks, less December

The year still running, on the NO2 page too: in grey at the end of the yearly means, its caption and the line under the figure saying the day it reaches. However much of it was measured it is drawn apart — a mean of part of a year, with the winter still to come, which the share of hours alone would stop marking in October. The portal is asked for the last day each row reaches, so the year can say where it ends. Both sources build a year's files one way for a whole year and for one so far, and a day is said without its year in one place; a test holds that a figure and the line under it say how far the year reaches in the same words

hot-nights: the page's question as a tool, so an agent can ask the measurements and the counts themselves. Days of a kind — tropical and torrid nights, hot and torrid days, frost, rain — counted year by year from the same histograms the page draws, at one station or at every one side by side, a threshold moved off the kind's, the months asked for counted from 1 as people count them. Each year says whether it was measured whole, the year still running says the day it reaches, the two halves of the record are compared as the page compares them, and the station's most extreme day comes with its date. Shown, the page is put the same question — station, kind, threshold, months — and every list and the slider say so. A tool reads the files the site serves, as a still reads them at build time, and a station whose file does not arrive is left out rather than failing the rest

no2: the page's measurements as a tool, so an agent can ask them and the sums made of them. A station, a run of years, which days of the week: the mean of them, hour by month, where it is highest and lowest, the mean of every year with the year still running marked by the day it reaches — and one hour of one month, or one row of the table, when the question is that narrow. Every station side by side ranks them on the last year all of them could have finished, never on the year still running. Hours are numbered 1 to 24 as the network numbers them, and the tool says, as the page does, that it does not say by which clock. Shown, the page is put the same question, and its lists say so

Hot nights opens on torrid nights, the nights at 25 °C or more, and the tool answers about them when an agent names no kind. A tropical night is most of a city summer by now, and the nights at 25 °C are where a record moves most: at Badalona 1.3 a year became 6.4, and 2026 had 33 by the end of September. The default lives in one place, the first kind in the list, from which the page's first question, its list and the tool's default all follow; the page and the projects list say 25 °C, and tell the reader to move the threshold down to 20 °C for the tropical ones

platform/blueprint: what a blueprint is, and how one runs. A blueprint is a program drawn as boxes and wires, the way Unreal and Unity draw theirs: kinds of node, each a pure function from typed inputs to typed outputs, and wires from an output to an input, coloured by what flows along them — a number, some words, yes or no, a table, a dial's value, which takes the shape of whatever it is wired into. A run goes in the order the wires need, hands each node what the others gave, keeps what a node gave while its inputs are the very ones of the run before, says in words why a node failed, waits for a file still on its way, and holds back what follows either. A blueprint is only data, so it has a text, one node a line, `name = kind "Title" input: value … @ x y`, where a value that names a node is a wire from it: read with every problem said by its line, written back as it was read. A blueprint written without places is tidied into columns as the data flows, each node drawn towards the nodes its wires join. And the nodes every blueprint has: a dial, the steps that work on any table — keep rows, sort, top, group, join on the keys both tables have, stack, a formula read by recursive descent and never by eval, the season taken out — the statistics — a summary, Pearson's and Spearman's correlation, a trend a decade, a histogram — the pictures, drawn as markup the same at build time and in the browser, each keyed so it can move — bars on zero, lines broken where years are missing, a scatter with its fitted line, a heat map mixed into the paper in the theme's colours, a table, a number — a note, and a table of one's own, pasted. Every table carries who measured it, and every picture says so under it

Blueprints can name this site's data: a feature brings kinds of node, and wires of its own, as it brings programs and tools. The weather brings its stations month by month, the days of a kind a year — torrid nights, frost, heavy rain, the threshold moved if asked — and the stations themselves; the air its measuring points by month, by year, by the hour of the day, and the points themselves; the source its own graph at any commit, the history a row a commit, measures as columns — PageRank, bridges, reach, core, stack, closeness, clustering, the group the arrows make, how often and how lately a file changed — steps — only some files, around a file, the knot, into boxes — its files and its arrows as tables, the network's figures, and its picture, in boxes or tangled, each ball as big as one column and coloured by another. A graph wired where a table is taken is the table of its files. Every source credits whoever measured it and says how old the copy is, and the year still running is waited for while it is on its way. A page writes a blueprint as a fenced block named after its place, ```::blueprint, its lines handed to the still — a test holds the markdown, the build and the still to what a place hands over: the build runs it on the very files the browser will fetch and writes its board — dials, pictures, captions, credits — the blueprint drawn as the canvas draws it, and its text. The content test runs every blueprint a page writes and holds that every line is read and every node answers. The plugin box now needs the blueprint's, which needs nothing but the escaping of markup: the arrow from the plugin box to the program's no longer goes against stability, and two more files are imported by a test

projects/blueprints: the site's data, wired by hand, the way Unreal and Unity wire their programs. A blueprint written in a page becomes, in the browser, a canvas and a board: nodes with a header in the colour of what they are for, typed pins and wires in the colour of what flows along them, each input written in place while no wire feeds it; drag from a pin to wire it, drop the wire in empty space and the menu offers only what it could go into, and stands the chosen node there, wired; double-click or the space bar for any node; drag a node by its title, the canvas to move about, Ctrl and the wheel to zoom, Shift to choose several, Delete, Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+D; ◉ puts a value on the board as a dial, turned there as the input it drives is written — a slider along the history says the day of each commit. Every edit runs the blueprint again, only what changed, the pictures redrawn in place so a bar that grows is seen growing; the reader's version is kept in their browser, Reset goes back, Link copies a link that opens it as it is, Text shows and takes it as text, Full screen gives it the window. It runs only once it is near the screen, keeping the board the build wrote until its data is here. Nine to start from: nights that do not cool, a working day in NO2, thirty years of every measuring point, whether the heat goes with the NO2 — as measured, the season taken out, the years taken out too — the files everything needs, what changes against what is needed, the groups the arrows make, the source grown commit by commit, and a table of your own. The browser's flag storage moves into the flags box, beside the store it keeps: the browser box, which the workbench made more stable, no longer needs a less stable one

Every program of the site is a node of a blueprint as well: read a fifth way, its parameters are its inputs, written as its dials are — a range, a choice, said as the program says them — the figures of its answer its outputs, found in the answer it gives when told nothing, however deep it keeps them, a list of them a table, and the picture of its own page is painted on the board. A figure that is none this time is no value, not a zero. So the simulation of technical debt can be turned by a dial and its months set beside anything else the site measures: the page has that as its tenth blueprint, the two roads drawn again from the months it gives back, and the month the clean one overtakes. Lines can draw a second column beside the first, the legend naming both

Blueprints as a tool, for an agent in the reader's browser: it writes one as text, the way the page writes its examples — the tool's description says how, with every kind there is and what each takes — and is answered with what every node said, the numbers each gave, and the tables the pictures were drawn from, the files it needs fetched as it finds it needs them. Shown, the blueprint goes onto the first canvas of the blueprints page as an edit, Undo and Reset still there. A dial with a range has a ▶ that plays it to its end, so the source can be watched growing commit by commit; and a ? beside the toolbar says what the hands do, on a page where full screen hides the page's own words. A page that makes a program's place as a fenced block is a page that shows it

A picture's legend stands under it, in as many rows as its names need inside the picture's width, and the picture is made taller for it: eleven measuring points in one line ran out of the picture and over the card beside it. On a phone, where a picture is drawn a third of its size, its words are drawn bigger to make up for it, and the canvas, there to be opened full screen, takes less of the page
